opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is that most robotic sensors today were designed for a world before large models. Cameras were built for human viewing, so they optimize for things like pleasing color and resolution at a fixed frame rate. Force sensors and encoders were built for classical control loops, where an engineer hand-designs what each signal means. Neither of those assumptions holds anymore.

If the downstream consumer is a learned model, a few things change.

First, the sensor should serve the model's representation, not a human's eyes. A model doesn't care whether an image looks nice. It cares about whether the signal carries the information it needs: depth, motion, contact, material properties. So you start to see value in sensors that output things like event streams, raw sensor data before the ISP processing, or multi-spectral signals that a person would never want to look at but a network can use very well.

Second, scale and consistency matter more than peak precision. Foundation models get their power from huge amounts of data. If every robot has a slightly different camera, different calibration, different mounting position, the data becomes fragmented and hard to pool. I'd actually trade some per-unit precision for standardization, cheap reproducibility, and good self-calibration, because that's what lets data from thousands of robots be trained on together. In a sense, the sensor becomes part of the data pipeline, not only part of the hardware.

Third, touch is the big gap. Vision we have from the internet, from video, from simulation. But contact-rich manipulation, like how hard you're gripping, whether something is slipping, how soft a material is, that information basically doesn't exist at scale. I think tactile sensing is where model needs should push hardware hardest: skins that are durable, cheap enough to cover a whole hand, and that output something a model can align with vision. Today a lot of tactile sensors are lab prototypes that break after a few thousand grasps. That's not compatible with collecting the kind of data a foundation model needs.

Fourth, the sensor and the model should be designed together. There's an idea I find appealing: rather than fixing the sensor and then training the model, you treat parts of the sensing pipeline as learnable, or at least co-optimized. Where do you put the cameras? What resolution and frame rate does the policy actually need? Maybe you need very high temporal resolution near the gripper and much less elsewhere. Those questions can be answered empirically by the model, instead of by intuition.

And finally, alignment with human data. One of the cheapest sources of manipulation data is people: egocentric video, gloves, wearables. If the robot's sensors are designed so their viewpoint and modalities match what we can capture from humans, then human data transfers to robots much more easily. That's a design constraint the sensor community didn't think about before, but it may end up being one of the most important.

So in short: sensors used to be designed for humans or for hand-written controllers. The next generation should be designed for learning, meaning information-rich, standardized, scalable, and especially much better at capturing touch and physical interaction.

r001.rationale: The response says sensor choices should serve the model’s information needs and that model evaluation can determine requirements such as camera placement, resolution, and frame rate. It also gives a concrete tradeoff: favor standardization and reproducibility over some per-unit precision.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because for most of the history of robotics the relationship ran the other way. We designed sensors first, based on what was physically convenient or cheap to build, and then we asked the algorithms to make sense of whatever came out. Cameras were built for human eyes, lidar was built to produce clean point clouds that an engineer could look at and verify, and the learning system was an afterthought. I think that order has to flip.

If you start from the model, the first thing you notice is that a large model does not actually want clean, pre-processed, human-readable data. It wants raw signal, high bandwidth, and good time alignment. A lot of the processing that happens inside a sensor today, things like ISP pipelines that make images look nice, auto exposure, denoising, and even the conversion of lidar returns into points, is throwing away information that a model could have used. So one direction I would push is sensors that expose more of the raw physics and let the model decide what matters.

The second thing is multimodality by design. Right now, fusing vision, touch, audio, proprioception, and force is a software problem, and it is painful because every sensor has its own clock, its own frame rate, its own latency. If the model is going to reason jointly over all of these, the hardware should make that easy, with shared timestamps, consistent spatial calibration, and ideally co-located sensing. I am particularly excited about touch here. Vision has had decades of investment, but a robot hand that cannot feel is working blind in exactly the moments that matter most, when it makes contact with the world. Dense, cheap, durable tactile skin is probably the single biggest gap between what models are capable of and what bodies can give them.

Third, I think we should think of sensors as part of the data engine, not just part of the robot. Models are hungry, and the bottleneck in embodied AI is data, not architecture. So a good sensor stack is one that produces data that is useful for training, not only for inference. That means low noise, good coverage of the interesting parts of the world, and formats that are easy to pool across many robots and even across different robot bodies. If every company ships its own exotic sensor with its own quirks, the data never adds up. There is real value in some degree of standardization.

And last, I would say we should let the model push back on cost. If a foundation model can recover depth from a few cameras well enough for manipulation, maybe you do not need the expensive depth sensor. If it can infer force from motor current and visual cues, maybe you can simplify the wrist. The model becomes a way to spend hardware budget on the things that are genuinely hard to infer, and skip the ones that are not. That is a very different design philosophy from building the most accurate sensor in isolation. The sensor and the model should be co-designed, and I think the labs that figure out how to do that loop quickly will end up ahead.

r001.rationale: The response says sensors should be designed starting from the model’s needs, prioritizing raw signal, bandwidth, timing alignment, and useful training data, while spending hardware budget on capabilities that are hard for the model to infer.

astra-6.text:
I think we should start with what the AI model needs to understand and do, then work backward to the sensors. A sensor can produce very high-resolution data, but if that data arrives too late or doesn’t capture the information needed for a decision, it may not help the robot very much.

Take grasping an object. Vision can help the robot locate it and estimate its shape, but knowing whether it’s slipping requires a different kind of feedback. That pushes us toward combining vision, touch, and force sensing, with good synchronization and low latency.

The other part is learning. We need sensor outputs that are consistent enough for models to learn from across different robots and environments. Calibration, reliability, and how uncertainty is represented matter alongside resolution.

So I’d treat the model, the sensors, and the control system as one design problem. The question is: what information will let this robot make a better decision, and how efficiently can we deliver it?

r001.rationale: The response says to start with what the AI model needs and work backward, then gives examples of prioritizing timely, decision-relevant data and low latency over resolution alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should start with what the AI model needs to understand and do, and then work backward to the sensors. For a robot, capturing a beautiful image is not necessarily the same as capturing useful information. The model needs observations that help it estimate the state of the world, recognize uncertainty, and choose an action.

That means evaluating sensors as part of the whole system. If a robot is manipulating an object, for example, vision might tell it where the object is, but touch can tell it whether the object is slipping. Timing and synchronization matter too: a very accurate measurement that arrives too late may be less useful than a simpler measurement delivered immediately.

I would like to see models and sensors developed together. We should ask which measurements actually improve task performance, how much processing should happen near the sensor, and how the system behaves when a signal is missing or unreliable. The goal is not simply more data. It is the right information, at the right time, so the robot can act reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says to start with what the model needs and work backward, then evaluate which measurements improve task performance. Its example weighs measurement accuracy against delivery time, communicating that model and task needs should guide sensor metric priorities.
